name: The House With No Fire

severity_by_style.why: The chimney is often the entrance front's principal vertical accent, at a sixth of the elevation's width.
The plan pinwheels about a massive central masonry chimney which is the tallest and heaviest element of the composition.
The stack is the structural and compositional centre; without it the ridge is unbroken and the house has no centre.
The hearth organises the plan and the stack continues the stone or clinker-brick base.
Paired stacks terminate a symmetrical roof that has no other event on it.
One central stack breaking the ridge forward of its midpoint is a defining tell of the type.
The revival was always looser, and a single end stack satisfies it.
Many were built with a small furnace flue and no fireplace at all.

severity_trajectory: Static in appearance, but the option closes: a chimney is the one element that cannot be added later without a footing, a structural opening through two floors and a roof, so a house built without one is built without one permanently.
symptom: A Tudor Revival, Cape, Georgian, Craftsman or Prairie house with no chimney at all: an unbroken roof, a mechanical flue on the rear slope, and either a direct-vent fireplace venting through a sidewall or nothing. The trim may be exemplary and the composition still has a hole in it, because the massing was designed around a vertical that is not there.

cause.explanation: An all-electric or heat-pump house has no combustion appliance to vent. Direct-vent gas fireplaces vent horizontally through a sidewall. And energy codes increasingly treat a masonry chimney as a thermal bridge and an air-leakage path that has to be sealed, insulated and blower-door tested around, so the cheapest compliant answer is not to have one. Three separate code and market pressures converge, and none of them has a line for what the chimney was doing compositionally.
cause.cost_saved: $10,000-25,000 including the footing, plus a measurable improvement in the blower-door result.

rule_violated.statement: Chimney breadth at least 1/6 of the elevation it sits on; stack height at least 3 ft above the ridge - the chimney is a principal element of the entrance front, not an accessory.
Plan pinwheeling about a massive central masonry chimney, which is the tallest and heaviest element of the composition.
Two, paired and symmetrically disposed - the terminating verticals of a symmetrical composition whose roof has no other incident.

Building thermal envelope air sealing, verified by blower door. A masonry chimney is a thermal bridge and a leakage path that has to be sealed, insulated and tested around, so the cheapest compliant answer is not to have one - which is how an energy code deletes a compositional element.

correct_practice: For most styles a lost chimney is a genuine and acceptable modern casualty. For a specific set it is fatal, because the massing was composed around the stack and there is nothing else to carry the vertical: Tudor Revival, where the chimney is often the entrance front's principal accent at a sixth of the elevation's width; Prairie School, where the plan turns around a central masonry mass that must be the heaviest object present; Craftsman, where the hearth organises the plan and the stack continues the stone or clinker-brick base; Cape Cod and First Period, where the stack is the structural and compositional centre; and Georgian, where paired stacks terminate a symmetrical roof that has no other event on it. On these, either build a real chimney doing real work, or choose a style whose massing does not depend on one.

fixes.right: A masonry chimney serving a wood-burning fireplace or stove, positioned by the plan.
fixes.cheap: Gather every mechanical vent the house actually has - furnace or boiler flue, water heater, radon stack, plumbing vents, range and dryer where they can be combined - and run them up through ONE masonry-dimensioned chase in the historically correct position, capped properly. It is a real duct doing real work, it is honest, it removes half a dozen pipes from the roof, and it restores the massing for the price of the chase.
fixes.dishonest: A shallow decorative chimney breast applied to a gable wall that stops at the eave. It claims a hearth and delivers neither the mass nor the vertical.

test.note: Binary, and the right shape for this fault: the question is whether the composition has the vertical it was designed around. On a Georgian the threshold is 2, symmetrically placed.

secondary_tests.note: The Tudor Revival rule - chimney breadth at least one sixth of the elevation it stands on. Absent or under a sixth is the fault on that style. SCOPED 24 Aug 2026 (OQ 41): this test's own first words are 'The Tudor Revival rule', and check_measurements reports a fault present when ANY of its tests fails -- so a Cape Cod colonial with two chimneys was failed for not having a Tudor one, and the finding it produced was reported against a parti named cape-central-chimney.

The Prairie test. If the chimney is not the visually heaviest object present, the composition has been inverted. SCOPED 24 Aug 2026 (OQ 41): 'The Prairie test', as this note already said. A chimney that is not the visually heaviest object in the composition is the fault on a Prairie house and is the normal condition on every other style this fault applies to.

detection: Look at the roofline for a vertical incident, then check against the style. On a Georgian, count: there should be two, symmetrically placed. On a Tudor Revival, measure the widest visible chimney face against the elevation's width - under a sixth, or absent, is the fault. On a Prairie house, if the chimney is not the visually heaviest object in the composition, the composition has been inverted. On a Cape, if the ridge is unbroken the house has no centre.

exceptions.why: The FHA-era type often had only a small furnace flue and no fireplace at all; a chimneyless example is historically accurate.
exceptions.bounds: A small flue expressed as a flue is correct; the type does not want a monumental stack either.

bounds_test.note: A small flue expressed as a flue is correct; the type does not want a monumental stack either.

exceptions.why: Post-hearth by construction date; many were built with metal flues from the start.
exceptions.bounds: Where a fireplace exists it should be expressed as a broad low masonry mass, which is the type's own idiom.

bounds_test.note: Where a fireplace exists it should read as a broad low masonry mass, which is the type's own idiom.

exceptions.why: Stove flues rather than chimneys, and often none surviving.
The type's composition is carried by the cantilevered balcony and the wall-plane step, not by a stack.
exceptions.bounds: A small stucco or brick stack is still expected; it is simply not load-bearing compositionally.

bounds_test.note: A small stucco or brick stack is still expected; it is simply not load-bearing compositionally.

confused_with.difference: The opposite response to the same cause. One builds nothing; the other builds a box. The box is usually worse.
